title: A Restless Night: Identifying and Managing a Sleep Disorder
learning_goal: Learners will understand how disruptions in specific sleep stages—particularly REM sleep and slow-wave NREM sleep—relate to observable symptoms, and how a clinician uses that knowledge to identify and manage a sleep disorder.
target_audience: Undergraduate psychology students and healthcare training professionals
visual_style: 2D semi-flat limited animation. Clean lines, muted but warm color palette. Characters express emotion through head turns, eyebrow movement, hand gestures, and subtle posture shifts. Mouth movement suggests speech without full phoneme matching. Backgrounds are detailed but static. Consistent lighting and proportions across all scenes.

appearance.uniform: White lab coat over a dark teal blouse, small silver stud earrings, lanyard with ID badge
appearance.distinguishing_features: Wire-rimmed rectangular glasses, calm and attentive expression

appearance.hair: Dark brown, short and slightly disheveled

scenes.setting: A quiet psychiatric outpatient office. A desk sits to one side with a computer monitor showing a patient file. Two chairs face each other at a slight angle near a window with soft natural light. A small whiteboard on the wall has a simple diagram of sleep stages. Morning ambience.
scenes.character_actions: Dr. Osei sits across from Marcus, holding a clipboard with notes. Marcus sits forward slightly, elbows on knees, looking tired. Dr. Osei glances at her clipboard, then looks up attentively. Marcus rubs the back of his neck as he speaks.

camera.angle: Medium two-shot, slightly elevated to show both characters equally
camera.movement: Slow pan left to settle on a balanced framing of both characters
camera.lens_effect: Slight warmth filter, soft focus on background

dialogue.line: I've been waking up two or three times every night for the past month. By morning I feel like I haven't slept at all, even when I'm in bed for seven or eight hours.
Thank you for tracking that. Does your partner ever mention that you snore loudly or seem to stop breathing during the night?
She has mentioned snoring, but she hasn't said anything about me stopping breathing. Mostly she says I toss around a lot and sometimes yell out.

audio.sound_effects: Subtle paper shuffle as Dr. Osei reviews clipboard
audio.ambience: Quiet office, faint ambient hum of ventilation, distant muffled hallway sounds

scenes.setting: Same outpatient office. Dr. Osei has turned slightly toward the whiteboard, which now has a simple hypnogram sketch showing sleep stage cycles.
scenes.character_actions: Dr. Osei gestures toward the whiteboard diagram with an open hand. Marcus looks toward the board, brow slightly furrowed in concentration. Dr. Osei turns back to face Marcus and nods reassuringly.

camera.angle: Medium shot favoring Dr. Osei, whiteboard visible in background
camera.movement: Gentle cut-in to whiteboard, then cut back to two-shot

dialogue.line: The yelling and physical movement at night are important clues. Healthy REM sleep involves a kind of natural muscle paralysis, so voluntary movement shouldn't happen during that phase.
So something is going wrong during REM sleep specifically?

scenes.setting: Same outpatient office. Dr. Osei has a printed sleep stage diagram on her clipboard and holds it up briefly for Marcus to see. The whiteboard now shows a simplified diagram labeling NREM stages 1, 2, and 3, alongside REM.
scenes.character_actions: Dr. Osei points to the diagram on the whiteboard, using her finger to trace from stage 1 through stage 3 and into REM. Marcus leans forward to look. Dr. Osei lowers the clipboard and gestures with her hands to illustrate depth of sleep. Marcus nods slowly, processing the information.

camera.angle: Over-the-shoulder shot from behind Marcus, showing Dr. Osei and whiteboard
camera.movement: Slow zoom in slightly on whiteboard diagram, then pull back to medium two-shot

dialogue.line: Sleep normally moves through several stages. The early stages of NREM sleep are lighter, but stage 3 is deep slow-wave sleep—the most restorative phase, with low-frequency, high-amplitude brain waves.

Then we cycle into REM sleep, where brain activity looks almost like wakefulness, and that's typically when dreaming occurs. The muscle paralysis during REM is what prevents us from acting out dreams.
So if that paralysis isn't working correctly, a person could actually move around or yell during a dream?

Exactly. That condition is called REM sleep behavior disorder. It's also worth noting that fragmented sleep like yours disrupts how much deep NREM and REM sleep you actually get, which explains why you don't feel rested even after many hours in bed.

audio.sound_effects: Pen tap on clipboard, light paper rustle
audio.ambience: Quiet office, consistent low ambient hum

scenes.setting: Same outpatient office. Dr. Osei is writing something on her notepad. Marcus sits back slightly, posture a little more relaxed than before, as if relieved to have a possible explanation.
scenes.character_actions: Dr. Osei finishes writing and looks up at Marcus. Marcus listens attentively, hands loosely clasped in his lap. Dr. Osei holds out the notepad briefly as she speaks.

camera.angle: Medium close-up on Dr. Osei, then cut to medium shot of Marcus, then back to two-shot
camera.movement: Subtle cuts between characters during dialogue

dialogue.line: Based on what you've described, I'd like to refer you for a sleep study so we can observe your brain wave activity and muscle tone across all the sleep stages through the night.
That makes sense. I had no idea that different stages of sleep could explain so much about how I'm feeling.

scenes.setting: Same outpatient office, slightly later in the appointment. Dr. Osei has set her clipboard aside and is speaking directly to Marcus in a more conversational tone. The whiteboard is still visible in the background.
scenes.character_actions: Dr. Osei leans forward slightly, using open-handed gestures to illustrate her points. Marcus listens and occasionally nods. At one point he raises a hand slightly to ask a question. Dr. Osei responds with a nod and a brief gesture toward the whiteboard.

camera.movement: Minimal movement; gentle cut between speaker and listener

dialogue.line: While we wait for the sleep study results, there are some behavioral steps that can support better sleep quality. Keeping a consistent sleep and wake schedule helps stabilize your biological clock.
I've been pretty inconsistent with my schedule lately—sometimes staying up past midnight and then trying to sleep in on weekends.
That inconsistency can fragment your sleep cycles. Also, avoiding caffeine and stimulating activities in the hour before bed reduces arousal levels that can delay sleep onset.
I do usually have coffee after dinner. I didn't think it was affecting anything because I still fall asleep, just not well.

Falling asleep is only part of the picture. Staying in each stage long enough to get full cognitive and physical restoration is the goal. Sleep deprivation accumulates and affects attention, memory, and decision-making significantly.

scenes.setting: Same outpatient office. Dr. Osei is standing slightly, preparing to wrap up the appointment. Marcus has straightened his posture and looks more engaged and less burdened than at the start of the scene.
scenes.character_actions: Dr. Osei hands Marcus a printed information sheet. Marcus takes it and glances down briefly, then looks back up. Both characters exchange a brief nod. Dr. Osei gestures toward the door in a welcoming, unhurried way.

camera.angle: Medium two-shot, slightly lower angle to convey a sense of resolution
camera.movement: Slow gentle pull back to take in the full setting
camera.lens_effect: Subtle warm tone to signal a constructive close

dialogue.line: I've written down the behavioral recommendations we discussed, along with what to expect from the sleep study. Treatment will depend on what the study shows, but identifying the affected stages is the starting point.
Thank you. Understanding that it's not just about hours of sleep, but about what's happening in each stage—that actually helps a lot.
